extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism; media studies readers and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and analyzing the occupational and processual ideologies that shape journalism practice, including the core professional values, how they are applied across cultures, and how ideology functions to legitimize, exclude, and maintain the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational ideology (definition — shared ideas ordering group life)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ideology" has two related definitions: a set of shared ideas that order group life... Following the first definition, an occupational ideology refers to a system of beliefs characteristic of a particular group of workers, including but not limited to their processes of producing meanings and ideas within the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion to identify the shared beliefs, practices, norms and meaning-producing processes that bind news workers together. Look for statements of collective values, routines, professional norms and sensemaking practices in news organizations when assessing occupational ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology as power relations (definition — constructing meanings in service of power)
rubrics_metrics.description: In its second definition, ideology is a process of constructing meanings in the service of power. News ideology is a global factor influencing journalistic decision-making, and scholars analyze how symbolic content in the news media connects with larger social interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how news narratives, framing, and definitions of 'real journalism' serve broader power structures; look for mechanisms where ideology advances particular interests, privileges some voices, or links news content to social/political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization as an ideological process
rubrics_metrics.description: In the course of the twentieth century, the professionalization of news media work consolidated thinking among journalists in different countries. Journalism scholars see professionalization as a distinctly ideological process that refines a consensus about who is a real journalist and what parts of news media qualify as real journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessatory focus: how professional norms, credentialing, and definitional debates are used to legitimate insiders and exclude outsiders; identify informal barriers to entry and how they are justified via professional discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant (isomorphic) occupational ideology of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Research suggests that news workers around the world have in common an occupational ideology consisting of a generally shared system of ideal-typical values. Regardless of cultural specificities, the existence of an increasingly isomorphic news ideology has consistently been documented in international journalism studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating journalism across contexts, look for common, recurrent value-claims and routines (even if applied differently); use cross-cultural comparison to detect both the shared core and local adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public service
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists provide a public service as watchdogs or newshounds, active collectors and disseminators of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative criterion for news work: does the reporting serve the public interest, perform watchdog functions, and actively collect and disseminate important information rather than merely entertain or promote special interests?

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: They strive to be impartial, neutral, objective, fair, and (thus) credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of neutrality and fairness critically: what does 'objectivity' mean in context (e.g., protection from marketers in the U.S. vs. using market values to resist political control in China)? Evaluate procedures and practices that are invoked to demonstrate impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: They must be autonomous, free, and independent to do their work effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional and editorial independence from political and commercial pressures. Check for structural protections (legal, organizational) and everyday practices that enable or undermine autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: They have a sense of immediacy, actuality, and speed inherent in the concept of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use timeliness and responsiveness as part of quality assessment: does coverage prioritize up‑to‑date reporting and a sense of happening-now? Balance speed against accuracy and context when judging immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics, validity, and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: They have a sense of ethics, validity, and legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ethical standards, fact-checking, sourcing, and legitimacy claims. Look for explicit ethical codes, adherence to verification practices, and how journalists justify the legitimacy of their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology as legitimizing/exclusionary mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: By legitimating self-appointed arbiters of professional debates and by excluding sources, stakeholders, and audiences from positions of power, news ideologies also serve to advance the status and internal coherence of an occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whose voices are authorized or marginalized by professional discourse; examine processes that confer authority (expert selection, gatekeeping) and practices that exclude or silence others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ideology to police responses and maintain control
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors use news ideology as a strategic ritual to position themselves in the profession and in relation to media critics and the audience. When faced with criticism, journalists apply ideological values to police themselves or to legitimate their recurring selections and descriptions of events and views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for rhetorical and ritualized uses of professional values when journalists respond to critique—claims to objectivity, independence, public service, etc.—and evaluate whether such invocations are substantive or defensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deployment of ideological values to manage debates about change
rubrics_metrics.description: News executives and journalists regularly revisit issues of commercialization, bureaucratization, new technology, audience declines, and ownership concentration. In all these debates, they deploy ideological values to maintain control on internal operations and to keep outside forces at bay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to examine how ideology is mobilized to respond to structural challenges (commercial pressures, technological change). Assess whether ideological claims enable adaptation, resist change, or protect incumbent interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of values despite internal contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists generally do not see inconsistencies or contradictions as they integrate these ideal-typical values into debates about the character of the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news practice, be alert to tensions (e.g., speed vs. accuracy, autonomy vs. market pressures). Note how journalists reconcile or ignore contradictions and how that affects credibility and practice.
